details:
**Minneapolis and St. Paul (the Twin Cities)**
St. Paul is Minnesota's capital, and Minneapolis is its largest city; together they form the Twin Cities metropolitan area on the Mississippi River, where most of the state's population lives. This is the standard giveaway.

**Lake Itasca**
A lake in north-central Minnesota recognized as the source of the Mississippi River. Visitors at Itasca State Park can wade across the river's tiny headwaters.

**Duluth**
A port city at the western tip of Lake Superior, near the Wisconsin border. It is a major shipping point for iron ore from the nearby iron ranges.

**Mesabi Range**
The largest iron ore range in the state, in the northeastern Arrowhead region. Its high-grade ore has run out, but low-grade taconite is still mined here, around towns such as Hibbing; the older Vermilion and Cuyuna Ranges are no longer active.

**Northwest Angle**
A piece of Minnesota north of the 49th parallel, cut off from the rest of the state by the Lake of the Woods, resulting from an error in early border treaties. It is the only part of the contiguous United States north of the 49th parallel and contains the site of the French Fort Saint Charles.

**"Land of 10,000 Lakes"**
Minnesota's nickname, referring to its many glacial lakes (it actually has more than 11,000 lakes of at least 10 acres).

**St. Anthony Falls**
The only major natural waterfall on the Mississippi River, located in Minneapolis. It powered the flour mills that made Minneapolis a major milling city.

**Voyageurs National Park**
Minnesota's only national park, centered on the Kabetogama Peninsula near the Canadian border. It is named after the French-Canadian fur traders (voyageurs) who traveled its waterways by canoe, and it lies west of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

**Mall of America**
One of the largest shopping malls in the United States, located in the Minneapolis suburb of Bloomington. Bloomington also submitted a bid to host the 2027 World's Fair.

**Fort Snelling**
A historic fort at the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers. During World War II it housed the Military Intelligence Service Language School, which trained soldiers in Japanese.

**Bde Maka Ska**
A lake in Minneapolis formerly named Lake Calhoun, after pro-slavery politician John C. Calhoun. It was renamed with its Dakota name, a change confirmed in 2020 after a court challenge.

**Eagle Mountain**
Minnesota's highest point, located in Cook County in the Arrowhead region. Minnesota's Cook County is not to be confused with Cook County, Illinois, home of Chicago.

**Somali community**
Minnesota, especially the Twin Cities, has the largest Somali population in the United States and one of the largest concentrations outside East Africa.

**Pipestone and Jeffers Petroglyphs**
Pipestone National Monument in southwest Minnesota preserves quarries of red pipestone (catlinite) used by Native Americans to carve sacred pipes. The nearby Jeffers Petroglyphs are ancient rock carvings on the same Red Rock Ridge.

**Minnehaha Falls and St. Urho's Day**
Minnehaha Falls is a waterfall in Minneapolis on Minnehaha Creek near its junction with the Mississippi. St. Urho's Day is a mock holiday honoring a fictional saint, invented in Minnesota and celebrated by Finnish Americans.
